name: NestJs
scope: A person with BASIC proficiency level in NestJs as a competency should be able to explain the NestJS mental model (modular, layered architecture, dependency injection, decorators, IoC), navigate standard project structure (`main.ts`, modules, controllers, services), create and organize modules, controllers, and services, define RESTful endpoints with route handlers and parameters, use DTOs with class-validator for validation and class-transformer for transformation, configure providers and dependency injection (singleton/request/transient scope, custom providers), bootstrap the app and set up global middleware, pipes, guards, interceptors, and exception filters, integrate with a database using TypeORM/Prisma/Mongoose for CRUD, implement basic JWT authentication and role-based authorization with Passport, manage configuration using `@nestjs/config` and environment variables, write and run basic unit/integration tests with Jest and `@nestjs/testing`, use logging via Nest Logger and understand basic monitoring, design simple REST APIs with correct HTTP methods/status, document APIs with `@nestjs/swagger`, use Nest CLI for code generation and development workflow, handle deployment basics (build, run, Docker, CI), and follow code quality, collaboration, and best practice guidelines for maintainable, secure, and testable NestJS projects.
long_scope:
{"sections":[{"name":"Core NestJS Mental Model & Framework Principles","scope_included":"- Understands NestJS as an opinionated Node.js framework built on TypeScript, emphasizing modular architecture, dependency injection, and decorators
- Understands how Nest wraps underlying HTTP platforms (Express by default, Fastify as alternative) and what that means for middleware and request handling
- Understands the high-level request lifecycle from incoming HTTP request → middleware → guards → interceptors (before) → pipes → controller/route handler → service calls → interceptors (after) → response → exception filters on errors
- Recognizes NestJS as layered / modular architecture (controllers → services → repositories/data access) and can keep responsibilities separated
- Understands the role of metadata and decorators (e.g., `@Controller`, `@Injectable`, `@Module`, method decorators for routes) as core to how Nest configures and wires the application
- Understands inversion of control (IoC) and dependency injection as primary way to manage dependencies rather than manually instantiating classes
- Understands synchronous vs asynchronous programming in NestJS (async/await, Promises) and how Nest handles async route handlers and providers
- Recognizes the advantages and tradeoffs of NestJS vs lighter frameworks (e.g., express) in terms of structure, maintainability, and learning curve","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Project Structure, Modules & Application Composition","scope_included":"- Can navigate and explain the structure of a standard Nest project (`main.ts`, `app.module.ts`, `app.controller.ts`, `app.service.ts`, etc.)
- Understands what a `Module` is in NestJS and how it is used to group related capabilities (controllers, providers, exports/imports) into cohesive units
- Can create feature modules and organize a medium-size application into modules based on domains or bounded contexts
- Understands root module vs feature modules and how module imports compose the overall application
- Knows how to declare `imports`, `controllers`, `providers`, and `exports` in a module and what each array does
- Can create shared or common modules for cross-cutting concerns (e.g., logging, configuration, utilities) and import them where needed
- Understands the difference between global modules and non-global modules, and knows when and how to register global modules
- Can handle circular dependency issues at a basic level (e.g., recognizing when they occur and using `forwardRef` in simple cases)
- Can split code logically into layers within a module (controller, service, repository or data access layer) and avoid putting business logic in controllers
- Understands how dynamic modules work conceptually (configuration-driven modules), even if only able to implement simple cases with documentation","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Controllers, Routing & Request Handling","scope_included":"- Can define controllers with the `@Controller()` decorator and configure route prefixes effectively
- Can create route handlers using method decorators like `@Get`, `@Post`, `@Put`, `@Patch`, `@Delete`, and `@All`
- Can use route parameters, query parameters, and request bodies via decorators like `@Param`, `@Query`, `@Body`, `@Req`, `@Res`, and `@Headers`
- Understands the difference between using the response object (`@Res()`) vs returning values from handler methods so Nest can handle responses automatically
- Can create RESTful endpoints with appropriate HTTP verbs and URL patterns, aligned with basic REST API design principles
- Can handle path parameters and nested routes (e.g., `/users/:userId/posts/:postId`) with proper parameter extraction
- Understands how to use `@HttpCode`, `@Header`, and `@Redirect` to control response metadata and status codes when needed
- Can use route-specific guards, pipes, interceptors, and filters via method-level decorators
- Can separate controller responsibilities from service logic, keeping controllers focused on request parsing, validation triggering, and response shaping
- Understands how to structure controllers for versioning at a basic level (e.g., path-based versioning) if required","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Providers & Dependency Injection","scope_included":"- Understands what a provider is in NestJS and that services, repositories, factories, and other classes are injected as providers
- Can create services using the `@Injectable()` decorator and register them in a module’s `providers` array
- Can inject provider dependencies into controllers and other providers via constructor injection
- Understands provider scope options (default singleton, request-scoped, transient) conceptually, and can configure basic scope where needed
- Knows how to define and inject custom providers, using `provide`/`useClass`/`useValue`/`useFactory`/`useExisting` for simple cases
- Understands how to inject values from configuration or external libraries into services using providers
- Recognizes when to abstract logic into reusable providers vs duplicating code in multiple services
- Understands basic token-based injection and can use injection tokens (including string or symbol tokens) in straightforward scenarios
- Can use `@Optional()` and partial dependency injection patterns in constrained cases
- Understands lifecycle of injected providers relative to application lifecycle in common singleton scenarios","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Application Bootstrap & Lifecycle","scope_included":"- Understands the purpose of `main.ts` and the Nest factory function (`NestFactory.create`) in bootstrapping the application
- Can configure base-level settings during bootstrap, such as global pipes, global filters, global interceptors, global guards, and global prefix
- Understands how to enable CORS for the application and configure simple CORS options
- Knows how to enable and use Nest’s built-in validation pipe globally for DTO validation
- Understands Nest application lifecycle hooks (`OnModuleInit`, `OnModuleDestroy`, `BeforeApplicationShutdown`, etc.) conceptually and can implement basic ones
- Can gracefully shut down the application and hook into shutdown signals for basic cleanup (e.g., closing database connections via provided integrations)
- Understands the difference between HTTP, microservice, and hybrid applications at a conceptual level, even if primarily working with HTTP","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"DTOs, Validation, and Data Transformation","scope_included":"- Understands the concept of Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) and why they are used to decouple external contracts from internal models
- Can define DTOs as TypeScript classes and decorate them with class-validator decorators (e.g., `@IsString`, `@IsInt`, `@IsEmail`, `@IsOptional`, `@IsEnum`, `@IsArray`)
- Can enable and configure `ValidationPipe` (globally and at route level) to validate incoming requests against DTOs
- Understands and can use `ValidationPipe` options such as `whitelist`, `forbidNonWhitelisted`, and `transform` to enforce payload constraints
- Can perform basic payload transformation using `class-transformer` decorators (e.g., `@Type`, `@Transform`) to coerce input types where necessary
- Can leverage DTOs for both incoming request bodies and outgoing response shapes where appropriate
- Understands common validation error structures and can return meaningful error messages to clients
- Knows how to handle nested DTO validation for objects and arrays in simple-to-moderate complexity payloads
- Avoids using raw `any` for request bodies and instead uses typed DTO classes for better type safety and maintainability","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Error Handling & Exception Filters","scope_included":"- Understands how Nest represents HTTP errors via `HttpException` and its subclasses (`BadRequestException`, `NotFoundException`, etc.)
- Can throw appropriate HTTP exceptions from controllers and services to signal domain or validation errors
- Understands how Nest’s default exception filter formats error responses and can reason about what clients will receive
- Can implement simple custom exception filters with `@Catch()` and use them at method, controller, or global level
- Can standardize basic error response structure across the application using global exception filters
- Understands differences between operational errors (e.g., invalid input, not found) vs programmer errors and where each should be handled
- Knows how to log errors in filters or interceptors to enable basic troubleshooting
- Can avoid leaking sensitive internal details in error responses and ensure user-friendly messages for client-facing APIs","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Middleware, Guards, Pipes, and Interceptors","scope_included":"- Understands middleware as pre-route logic operating at the Express/Fastify layer and can implement simple middleware functions or classes
- Can apply middleware to routes or route groups using module `configure` method and `MiddlewareConsumer`
- Understands guards as gatekeepers that determine whether a request is allowed to proceed (e.g., auth checks, role checks)
- Can implement basic guards using `CanActivate` and apply them with the `@UseGuards()` decorator at route and controller levels
- Understands pipes as transformation and validation mechanisms that run before route handlers, beyond simple DTO validation (e.g., parsing IDs, custom validation)
- Can develop simple custom pipes (e.g., parsing and validating route parameters) and apply them using `@UsePipes()` or parameter decorators
- Understands interceptors as wrappers around route execution that can modify incoming requests or outgoing responses, measure execution time, or add logging
- Can implement simple interceptors (e.g., logging, mapping responses) using the `NestInterceptor` interface
- Understands the typical order of execution for middleware → guards → interceptors → pipes → filters and can debug flow-related issues in simple cases","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Data Persistence & Database Integration","scope_included":"- Understands the role of ORMs/ODMs (e.g., TypeORM, Prisma, Mongoose) in NestJS and can integrate at least one commonly used library
- Can configure TypeORM or Prisma (or an equivalent) within a Nest module, including database connection options via environment/config
- Can define entities or models and wire them into repositories or services for CRUD operations
- Can inject repositories or database services into Nest services using DI for basic data-access
- Understands how to handle basic transactions or multi-operation workflows conceptually, even if using high-level abstractions
- Can implement basic pagination, filtering, and sorting logic at the data-access or service layer
- Knows how to avoid direct database calls in controllers and instead route all database operations through services or repositories
- Understands how to handle simple database errors (e.g., unique constraint violations) and translate them into appropriate HTTP responses
- Can structure data access code in a way that keeps business logic separated from persistence logic, even if not using advanced patterns","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Security, Authentication & Authorization (Basic Level)","scope_included":"- Understands common web API security concerns (authentication, authorization, input validation, basic rate limiting conceptually)
- Can implement basic JWT-based authentication using Passport and Nest’s AuthModule patterns (e.g., `@nestjs/passport`, `passport-jwt`)
- Can define and use strategies (e.g., `JwtStrategy`, potentially `LocalStrategy`) and wire them into guards (`AuthGuard('jwt')`)
- Understands how to protect routes with guards and differentiate between public and protected routes
- Can store and access authenticated user information from `Request` (e.g., `req.user`) or decorators (e.g., a custom `@User()` decorator)
- Understands simple role-based access control using metadata (e.g., `@Roles` decorator) and a roles guard, in at least straightforward scenarios
- Knows how to protect sensitive configuration values (JWT secrets, DB passwords) via environment configuration
- Understands basics of password handling (hashing with libraries like bcrypt) and never storing raw passwords in the database
- Can configure basic CORS settings to avoid common cross-origin issues while keeping security reasonably tight
- Understands at a conceptual level threats like XSS, SQL injection, and CSRF, and knows that Nest’s validation and parameterized queries/ORM help mitigate them","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"HTTP, REST API Design & Serialization","scope_included":"- Understands basic HTTP concepts (methods, status codes, headers, request/response body, content types)
- Can design and implement simple RESTful APIs with meaningful resource naming, appropriate HTTP verbs, and proper status codes
- Can return appropriate HTTP status codes for create (201), update (200/204), delete (204/404 where appropriate), etc., in common scenarios
- Can use Nest’s response serialization features (e.g., `ClassSerializerInterceptor`, `@Exclude`, `@Expose`) for simple response shaping
- Understands how to avoid exposing sensitive fields in responses and use DTOs or serialization decorators to control output
- Can implement basic versioning strategies conceptually (e.g., separate controller versions or path-based versioning) even if not deeply experienced
- Understands how to send and read common HTTP headers (auth headers, content-type, custom headers) within Nest controllers and services
- Recognizes when to return paginated responses and can design basic pagination response structures (items, total count, page info)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Configuration Management & Environment Handling","scope_included":"- Can use `@nestjs/config` or equivalent approaches to manage configuration across environments (development, testing, production)
- Can load configuration from `.env` files and environment variables, and provide defaults when appropriate
- Understands the difference between build-time vs runtime configuration and organizes values accordingly
- Can create configuration modules or services that expose typed configuration objects to the rest of the application
- Can perform basic validation of environment variables (e.g., using `Joi` with `ConfigModule`) before application bootstrap
- Knows how to avoid committing secrets to version control and understands basic secure management of configuration in local development
- Can configure database URLs, API keys, and JWT secrets using the configuration module and inject them where needed
- Can organize configuration by domain or feature (e.g., `database`, `auth`, `app`) to keep it maintainable","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Testing Fundamentals in a NestJS Context","scope_included":"- Understands the value of automated tests and basic testing terminology (unit, integration, e2e tests)
- Can use Nest’s testing utilities (`@nestjs/testing`) to set up simple unit tests for services and controllers
- Can configure a test module with mocked providers and dependencies for isolated unit testing
- Knows how to run tests with the default test runner (Jest in standard Nest setups) and interpret basic test results
- Can write basic tests that cover positive paths and simple error conditions for services and controllers
- Understands how to mock external services, repositories, or HTTP calls in tests using Jest mocks or similar mechanisms
- Can set up simple end-to-end tests against a running Nest application in-memory (using `Test.createTestingModule` and starting an HTTP server)
- Understands limitations of unit tests vs integration/e2e tests and knows where each is more appropriate in a Nest context","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Logging, Monitoring & Basic Observability","scope_included":"- Understands the purpose of logging in NestJS applications and can use Nest’s built-in `Logger` class for application logs
- Can add contextual logging in controllers, services, and key middleware/guards/interceptors for tracing basic flows
- Can adjust Nest’s log levels and configure simple logging options during bootstrap
- Understands how to log errors within exception filters or interceptors for later troubleshooting
- Has basic familiarity with integrating external logging/monitoring tools conceptually (e.g., sending logs to a centralized system), even if not implementing full setups independently
- Understands importance of correlation identifiers or request IDs conceptually and can propagate them through logs at a simple level if tooling is provided","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Performance & Scalability Basics (HTTP-focused)","scope_included":"- Understands that Nest apps can run on Express or Fastify and recognizes basic performance tradeoffs between them
- Understands importance of avoiding blocking operations on the event loop and using async I/O for database and network calls
- Can identify obvious performance anti-patterns (e.g., heavy computation in request handlers, unbounded loops, unnecessary serialization work)
- Understands basic caching concepts (in-memory cache, HTTP caching headers, simple key-based caches) at a conceptual level and can use simple Nest cache module setups with guidance
- Knows that horizontal scaling (multiple instances) is often handled outside Nest (e.g., via containers, orchestrators) and that Nest instances should remain stateless for this to work well
- Understands that large responses and chatty endpoints can affect performance and knows to design simpler, well-bounded endpoints when possible","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"API Documentation & Developer Experience (within Nest)","scope_included":"- Can integrate and configure auto-generated API documentation using `@nestjs/swagger` in standard scenarios
- Can add Swagger decorators (`@ApiTags`, `@ApiOperation`, `@ApiResponse`, `@ApiProperty`) to controllers and DTOs to describe endpoints and data models
- Can expose Swagger UI at a configured path and secure it in basic ways (e.g., restrict in production or protect with simple auth)
- Understands how API documentation helps internal and external consumers and keeps documentation roughly in sync with implementation
- Can contribute to maintaining accurate API docs as controllers and DTOs evolve
- Understands how Nest’s decorators can improve IDE support and type inference for API development","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Tooling, CLI Usage & Local Development Workflow","scope_included":"- Can use the Nest CLI (`nest` command) to generate modules, controllers, services, and other artifacts
- Understands Nest CLI workspace structure and common commands (`nest new`, `nest generate`, `nest build`, `nest start`, `nest test`)
- Can run the application in development mode with auto-reload (`nest start --watch` or equivalent tooling)
- Can configure basic TypeScript compiler options used by Nest (e.g., `tsconfig.json` settings relevant to decorators and metadata)
- Can use common package managers (npm, pnpm, yarn) to manage Nest-related dependencies and scripts
- Understands how to structure scripts in `package.json` for starting, building, testing, and linting Nest apps
- Can debug a NestJS application locally using IDE or editor debugging capabilities, breakpoints, and stack traces
- Has basic familiarity with using Postman/Insomnia/REST Client or similar tools to test HTTP endpoints during development
- Can work with Git or similar VCS to manage Nest projects and follow basic branching and commit practices","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Deployment, Environment Setup & Basic DevOps Integration","scope_included":"- Understands how to build a NestJS application for production (transpile TypeScript to JavaScript, use `nest build` or equivalent)
- Can configure environment-specific settings (e.g., different `.env` files or environment variable configurations) for dev, staging, and production
- Has basic familiarity with running NestJS applications in Node.js runtime (e.g., `node dist/main.js`) and configuring host/port
- Understands containerization concepts at a high level and can work with a simple Dockerfile or container image for a Nest service
- Can collaborate with DevOps or platform teams to expose health-check endpoints, readiness endpoints, and basic configuration needed for deployment
- Understands importance of logging to stdout/stderr for containerized environments and configures logs accordingly
- Can participate in setting up simple CI pipelines (install deps, run tests, build) for Nest projects, with guidance","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Code Quality & Best Practices in Nest Projects","scope_included":"- Writes code that follows Nest’s architectural patterns (controllers → services → repositories/data access) and avoids mixing concerns
- Refactors code to improve readability, modularity, and reusability within Nest modules as features evolve
- Follows team conventions for folder structure, naming, and module boundaries
- Participates in code reviews for NestJS codebases, can both give and receive constructive feedback on architecture, readability, and test coverage
- Uses TypeScript features effectively in Nest projects (interfaces, types, enums, generics where appropriate) to maintain type safety
- Adheres to linting and formatting rules (ESLint, Prettier) and can fix common issues reported by tooling
- Documents key parts of the Nest application (README updates, ADR notes, comments where necessary) to ensure maintainability
- Communicates clearly with frontend, mobile, or consuming-service teams about API changes, contracts, and versioning
- Collaborates with security, DevOps, and QA to ensure that Nest APIs meet basic security, reliability, and quality expectations
- Is open to adopting team-wide best practices for Nest usage (e.g., standard error formats, logging patterns, DTO conventions) and helps keep them consistent","is_non_core_section":true}]}
